Wikipedia, 'Bird's Opening' / 'Henry Bird (chess player)' (re-verified 2026-06-08): 'Named after 19th-century English player Henry Bird'; he played 1.f4 from 1855 for some forty years and the Hereford Times named it after him in 1885. The move predates him (mentioned by Lucena c. 1497; later La Bourdonnais and Elijah Williams).

Wikipedia, 'Nimzowitsch-Larsen Attack' (re-verified 2026-06-08): the 1.b3 opening 'is named for the Danish grandmaster Bent Larsen' and is also called 'Larsen's Opening'. Larsen played it frequently 1968-1972; earlier master exponents include John Owen (1870s) and Aron Nimzowitsch (1920s-30s), so the line predates him.

Wikipedia, 'Réti Opening' (re-verified 2026-06-08): 'The opening is named after Czechoslovak chess player Richard Réti (1889-1929)'; Hans Kmoch named the 'Réti System' after Réti-Rubinstein, Karlovy Vary (Carlsbad) 1923. The bare move 1.Nf3 predates Réti and is catalogued separately as the Zukertort Opening; the name marks his hypermodern treatment.
